## Block A — What a reservoir-to-river hydraulic transition means

### T01 — RETRIEVAL UNVALIDATED

> Reservoirs and rivers differ systematically in longitudinal water-surface geometry: impounded reaches tend towards low longitudinal gradients, whereas free-flowing reaches maintain persistent downstream gradients controlled by discharge, channel geometry, roughness and backwater conditions.

- **Manuscript anchor**: 1.2 Why post-breach water-surface geometry matters
- **Evidence (papers)**: 4 — 4 supporting (3 same-system own results), 0 contradicting, 0 method-relevant, 0 analogues
- **Evidence (passages)**: 5 supporting, 0 contradicting, 4 verified, 0 papers lost to unverifiable quotes, 7 filtered out before adjudication
- **Corpus coverage**: thin — 5 of 2615 candidate works present (ratio 0.00)
- **Retrieval validation**: 0/0 verified direct controls recovered · overall 0% · at expected stage 0% · semantic alone 0% · holdout 0%
- **Verdict rationale**: No hold-out positive control passed for this thesis, so a null result cannot be distinguished from a retrieval failure. Supply a verified positive control before reading anything into this row.
- **Established**: Evidence confirms that reservoirs and impounded reaches exhibit flattened longitudinal water-surface gradients [doi:10.3390/w15112057, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0068186]. Conversely, free-flowing rivers maintain gradients influenced by discharge and backwater effects [doi:10.1029/2025gl115953, doi:10.3390/rs16214010]. These distinct hydraulic characterisations demonstrate systematic differences in longitudinal geometry between impounded and natural riverine systems.
- **Still missing**: While the evidence supports the general distinction between impounded and free-flowing reaches, it lacks a comprehensive, comparative analysis that explicitly quantifies the systematic differences in longitudinal geometry across a broad range of global river systems.
- **Closest study** (SUPPORTS): SWOT Reveals Detailed Dynamics of Longitudinal River Slope in the Missouri River Basin ([10.1029/2025gl115953](https://doi.org/10.1029/2025gl115953), 2025)
  > Moreover, the longitudinal profiles from SWOT revealed significant backwater effects at the confluence of the Missouri and Yellowstone rivers.

- **Established**: Dam removal and reservoir drawdown trigger transitions from impounded to channelised fluvial regimes, causing increased flow velocity [doi:10.22230/jem.2009v10n1a412], channel incision [doi:10.1029/2006wr005621, doi:10.1029/2003wr002940], and knickpoint development [doi:10.25675/3.026556]. These processes alter hydro-morphodynamics and sediment transport [doi:10.2110/jsr.2018.61], though some studies suggest long-term geomorphic impacts may be limited in specific contexts [doi:10.1111/j.1752-1688.2008.00263.x].
- **Still missing**: The evidence lacks a comprehensive characterisation of the generalisability of these geomorphic responses across diverse river systems and dam types. - **Established**: Evidence confirms that discrepancies in height data often arise from the use of different vertical datums, geoids, and national height systems [doi:10.1093/gji/ggt161, doi:10.3390/rs14040920, doi:10.1007/s12210-020-00948-0].   > As TGs managed by national authorities are rigorously connected to the national height systems, the TG data can also be used in a common system.
